Pure functions
How to tell a pure function from an impure one in JavaScript and return a new object with spread or structuredClone instead of mutating outside data.
Learn to tell pure functions from impure ones and to rewrite impure ones so that they return a new value instead of mutating outside data.
text

Pure functions are extremely important. A pure function is not necessarily idempotent, though: x => x + 1 is pure, but applying it to its own result gives a new value. If you need side effects, group them into separate functions and keep them apart from pure functions. Every program, especially on the web, needs side effects (mutating the DOM tree, requests to the server (fetch), reading from a file (readFile), and so on).

A pure function is not necessarily idempotent: x => x + 1 is pure, but applying it to its own result gives a new value.
Every program, especially on the web, needs side effects: mutating the DOM, requests to the server, reading from a file. Group them into separate functions and keep them apart from pure functions.
A function that mutates an outer variable creates side effects: several functions may work with that variable, and a bug will be harder to track down.
A pure function does not change the object passed to it but returns a new one: with spread, or with structuredClone if deep cloning is needed.
Even in a module with its own closure, it is better to replace the state with a new object than to mutate it.

The addTagImpure function changes the post passed to it. Write a pure addTag: it returns a new post with the tag added and leaves the original alone. Keep in mind that tags is a nested array: if you copy only the object itself, the array stays shared.

The result of finalPriceImpure depends on the outer variable discount: with the same argument, the function returns a different price once discount has changed. Write a pure finalPrice that receives the discount percentage as an argument. Run the code and compare the lines before and after discount changes.
